nodes.characterization_summary: Cyclic voltammograms of Pt(110) in 0.1 M KOH and 0.1 M LiOH at 50 mV/s show HOH-X peak shift of approximately -15 mV from KOH to LiOH, indicating stronger OH binding in LiOH.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Voltammograms of Pt(110) in 0.1 M KOH, 0.1 M LiOH, and 0.1 M HCLO4 are shown in Figure 1a. ... the (110) peak shifts by approximately -15 mV from KOH to LiOH, indicating stronger OH binding in LiOH.

nodes.characterization_summary: Peak splitting ΔEp versus peak current density for HOH-X on Pt(110) shows reversible kinetics at pH 1 and slower HOH-X kinetics at pH 13 with greater ΔEp in LiOH than in KOH.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Figure 2 plots ΔEp versus peak current density ... for the HOH-X region of Pt(110). ... At pH 13, increasing ΔEp with scan rate shows slower HOH-X kinetics, with greater ΔEp in LiOH, indicating slower adsorption than in KOH.

nodes.characterization_summary: Currents normalized by ECSA calculated from H-UPD charge of 147 μC/cm² for Pt(110).
nodes.evidence_snippet: the currents are normalized by the electrochemical active surface area (ECSA), based on the traditional H-UPD method with the constant 147 μC/cm.

nodes.characterization_summary: Cyclic voltammograms of Pt(111) in 0.1 M KOH and 0.1 M LiOH show hydrogen region unaffected from KOH to LiOH while hydroxide adsorption potential changes.
nodes.evidence_snippet: On Pt(111), hydrogen and hydroxide adsorption are separated by ∼0.8 V, and while the hydrogen region remains unaffected from KOH to LiOH, there is a change in the adsorption potential of hydroxide species, as shown in Figure 1b.
